items.en: Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception: Its Name
items.zh: 非想非非想處 · 釋名

zh: 第四、釋非想非非想定，亦為三：一、釋名；二、修行方法；三、證相。一、釋名者，言非想非非想者，解釋不同。有言：此定名一存一亡觀，所言非想者，非麁想，此則亡於麁想。非非想者，非非細想，此則存於細想。又解云：前觀識處是有想，不用處是無想。今雙除上二想，非想遣識處有想，非非想遣不用處無想故。又解言：若非有想者，此定中不見一切相貌故。言非有想非無想者，行人或作是念：若一向無想者，如木石無知，云何能知無想？故言非無想也。
en: Fourth, explaining the concentration of neither perception nor non-perception: this too has three parts — explaining the name; the method of cultivation; and the mark of realization.

First, explaining the name: as for "neither perception nor non-perception," this is explained differently by different sources. Some say: this concentration is named the contemplation of one thing retained and one thing relinquished — as for "not perception," this means not coarse perception, this being what is relinquished, coarse perception; as for "not non-perception," this means not the absence of fine perception, this being what is retained, fine perception.

Another explanation says: the sphere of consciousness discussed earlier has perception present; the sphere of nothingness has no perception at all. Here, both of these two kinds of perception are simultaneously removed — "not perception" dispels the sphere of consciousness's own presence of perception, and "not non-perception" dispels the sphere of nothingness's own absence of perception.

A further explanation says: as for "not having perception," this is because, within this concentration, no mark or appearance whatsoever is seen. As for saying "neither perception nor non-perception": the practitioner might reflect: if it were an absolute absence of perception, this would be like wood or stone, without any awareness at all — how, then, could it possibly know that it is without perception? Hence it is said to be "not without perception" either.

zh: 問曰：非有想非無想中實有想，云何言無想耶？答曰：非想有四陰共成，豈得言無？但凡夫人入此定中，陰、界、入細故不覺，謂言無想。佛法中說有四陰共成，但因其本名，故言非有想非無想。亦有解言：約凡夫說，言非有想；約佛法中說，言非無想；合而論之，故言非有想非無想也。
en: Question: within "neither perception nor non-perception," perception is, in truth, genuinely present — how, then, can it be said to be "without perception"? Answer: this concentration of "neither perception" is itself made up of the four aggregates together — how, then, could it possibly be said to be entirely absent? It is simply that an ordinary person, entering this concentration, the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements being so fine, fails to perceive them, and so says there is "no perception" present. Within the Buddhadharma, it is said that the four aggregates together make up this concentration, but, following its own original name, it is still spoken of as "neither perception nor non-perception." There is also an explanation that says: spoken of with reference to the ordinary person, it is said to be "not having perception"; spoken of with reference to the Buddhadharma, it is said to be "not without perception" — taken together, it is thus spoken of as "neither perception nor non-perception."

The four competing etymologies offered without a forced choice among them is the treatise's characteristic move once again, but the substantive philosophical point underneath all four is sharper here than usual: a state can genuinely contain the four aggregates — and so, in the treatise's own technical sense, contain "perception" — while still feeling like the total absence of perception from within, simply because it has grown too fine for an untrained observer to detect. This is the same warning as the earlier aside on deviant no-thought concentration, now given its precise philosophical grounding: subjective absence of felt content is not the same as objective absence of mental activity.

items.en: Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception: Cultivation and Realization
items.zh: 非想非非想處 · 修行方法、證相

zh: 第二、修行方法，亦有二：一者、訶讚；二者、觀行修習。訶責者，深知無想中過罪，是無所有定，如癡如醉，如眠如暗，無明覆蔽，無所覺了，無可愛樂，故《摩訶衍》云：「觀於識處如瘡如箭，觀無想處如癡，皆是心病，非真寂靜處。更有妙定，名曰非想，是處安隱，無諸過罪，我當求之。」二、明觀行修習。行者爾時諦觀無所緣，受、想、行、識如病如癰，如瘡如刺，無常、苦、空、無我，欺誑不實，和合而有，非實有。如是觀已，即便捨離，心觀於非有非無。
en: Second, the method of cultivation: this too has two parts — reproach and praise; and analytic contemplation.

As for reproach: one deeply understands the fault within the concentration of no-thought — this concentration of nothingness resembles delusion, resembles intoxication, resembles sleep, resembles darkness, ignorance covering it over, nothing at all perceived clearly, nothing in it worth loving or delighting in — hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "Observing the sphere of consciousness as a wound, as an arrow; observing the sphere of nothingness as delusion — both are themselves illnesses of the mind, not a truly still place at all. There is a further, more subtle concentration, named 'neither perception,' where this place is truly secure, free of every such fault — I shall now seek it out."

Second, clarifying analytic contemplation. The practitioner, at this point, closely contemplates the object of nothingness: its sensation, perception, formation, and consciousness are themselves like an illness, like a boil, like a wound, like a thorn, impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, deceptive and unreal, arisen only through the coming together of causes and conditions, not truly existent at all. Having contemplated in this way, one relinquishes and leaves this behind, the mind now contemplating what is neither existent nor nonexistent.

zh: 何法非有？謂心非有。何以故？過去、現在、未來，求之都不可得，無有形相，亦無處所，當知非有。云何非無？若言是無，何名無為？心是無為，離心是無。若心是無，不名為心，以無覺無緣故；若心非無，更無別無。何以故？無不自無，破有故說無，無有則無無，故言非有非無。如是觀時，不見有無，一心緣中，不念餘事，是名修習非有想非無想定。如是即依非有非無，常念不捨，則不用處定便自謝滅，而非有想非無想定未發，於其中間亦如上說。
en: What dharma is "not existent"? The mind is said to be "not existent." Why is this? Sought throughout the past, present, and future, it can nowhere be found at all, having no form or mark, and no location either — hence it should be known as "not existent." How, then, is it "not nonexistent"? If it were said to be simply nonexistent, how could it then be named "unconditioned" at all? The mind is itself unconditioned; apart from mind, there is nonexistence. If mind itself were nonexistent, it could not be named "mind" at all, since it would then have no awareness and no object whatsoever; and if mind is not nonexistent, then there is no further, separate "nonexistence" to speak of either. Why is this? Nonexistence is not, in itself, self-subsisting — it is spoken of only in order to break through existence; and, once existence is gone, nonexistence, too, is gone along with it — hence it is said to be "neither existent nor nonexistent."

Contemplating in this way, seeing neither existence nor nonexistence, the mind held single-mindedly on this very object, taking up no other matter at all — this is named cultivating the concentration of neither perception nor non-perception. Continuing in this way, relying on what is neither existent nor nonexistent, holding this in mind constantly without relinquishing it, the concentration of nothingness thereupon passes away and is extinguished of itself, while the concentration of neither perception nor non-perception has not yet arisen; in this interval, the same holds as already described above.

zh: 第三、明證相，亦為六意：一者、正明證相；二、明支；三、明體用；四、明淺深；五、進退；六、功德。第一、明證相者，行者既一心專精，加功不已，其心任運，住在緣中，於後忽然真實定發，不見有無相貌，泯然寂絕，心無動搖，恬然清淨，如涅槃相。是定微妙，三界無過，外道證之，謂是中道、實相、涅槃、常、樂、我、淨，愛著是法，更不修習。彼若正觀，如步屈蟲行至樹表，更不復進，到退迴還。如經中說：「凡夫證此定法，如繩繫鳥，繩盡則還。」已其不知四陰和合而有自性。
en: Third, clarifying the mark of realization: this too has six parts — directly clarifying the mark of realization; clarifying the factors; clarifying substance and function; depth; progress and regression; and merit.

First, clarifying the mark of realization: the practitioner, single-mindedly devoted, applying effort without pause, the mind now abiding spontaneously within this object; afterward, suddenly, a truly genuine concentration is brought forth, seeing no mark of either existence or nonexistence at all, indistinct and utterly still, the mind free of any agitation whatsoever, tranquil and pure, resembling the very mark of nirvāṇa itself. This concentration is subtle and wondrous, unsurpassed within the three realms; non-Buddhist practitioners, realizing it, take it to be the middle way, the true mark, nirvāṇa itself, permanent, blissful, possessing self, and pure — clinging to this very dharma with attachment, and cultivating nothing further. Were they to contemplate it correctly, however, they would see it is like an inchworm crawling to the very tip of a branch, unable to advance any further, and forced to turn back the way it came. As the sūtra says: "When an ordinary person realizes this dharma of concentration, it is like a bird tied by a rope — once the rope has run its length, the bird is pulled back again." This is because they do not know that it exists only through the four aggregates combining together, and take it to have a nature of its own.

zh: 然其雖無麁煩惱，而亦成就十種細煩惱，以不知故，謂是真實，外道入此定中，不見有無，而覺有能知非有非無之心，即計此心謂是真神不滅，故言神至細，不破神能知。若佛弟子，知是四陰和合而有，虛誑不實，是中心想，故知無別神知。復次，前虛空處破色故說空，識處破空故說識，說識為有想，不用處破識故無識，說無識為無想。今此定破無所有，說非無想，故言非有想非無想。此定於世間中沈浮等故，智、定、空、有均平，是定安隱，於世間中最為尊勝，等智所不能破，故數人言：「一常有漏。」
en: And although such a person is free of coarse afflictions here, they are nonetheless still complete with ten kinds of subtle affliction — and, not knowing this, they take the state to be truly real. Non-Buddhist practitioners, entering this concentration, see neither existence nor nonexistence, and yet become aware of a mind that seems able to know this very neither-existence-nor-nonexistence — and, reckoning this very mind to be the true, imperishable spirit-self, they say that this spirit-self is exceedingly subtle, and cannot be shown to lack the capacity to know. A disciple of the Buddha, by contrast, knows that this, too, is nothing but the four aggregates combining together, deceptive and unreal, simply a state of mind occurring within it — and so knows there is no separate, knowing spirit-self present here at all.

Furthermore: the previous sphere of space breaks through form, and so is called "emptiness"; the sphere of consciousness breaks through emptiness, and so is called "consciousness," and consciousness is spoken of as having perception. The sphere of nothingness breaks through consciousness, and so is without consciousness, and this absence of consciousness is spoken of as "no perception." This present concentration breaks through nothingness itself, and so is spoken of as "not without perception" — hence it is called "neither perception nor non-perception." This concentration, relative to the mundane world, is evenly balanced, neither sinking nor rising — wisdom, concentration, emptiness, and existence all held in perfect equilibrium; this concentration is secure, the very most exalted and excellent within the mundane world, something ordinary, equanimous wisdom is unable to break through — hence the Abhidharma masters say: "This alone is forever contaminated."

zh: 復次，無想有三義：一、無想天定；二、非有想非無想定；三、滅受想定。無方便外道滅心，入無想天定；有方便凡夫外道滅心，入非有想非無想定；佛弟子滅心，入滅受想定。問曰：無所有處亦名無想定，何故不入三種滅心耶？答曰：不善滅無所有中心數法故非妙。復次，若在色界，無想為極；若在無色界，非有想非無想為極。若佛法中，自有滅、受、想，不用處於三處中皆非勝定，故不取也。第二、明支；三、體用；四、淺深；五、進退；六、功德，義類前可知。
en: Furthermore: "no-thought" carries three distinct senses: the concentration of the heaven of no-thought; the concentration of neither perception nor non-perception; and the concentration of the cessation of sensation and perception. The non-Buddhist practitioner without any proper skillful means, extinguishing the mind, enters the concentration of the heaven of no-thought; the ordinary, non-Buddhist practitioner with some skillful means, extinguishing the mind, enters the concentration of neither perception nor non-perception; and the Buddha's own disciple, extinguishing the mind, enters the concentration of the cessation of sensation and perception instead.

Question: the sphere of nothingness is also named the concentration of no-thought — why, then, is it not included among these three kinds of extinguished mind? Answer: it is because it does not properly extinguish the mental factors present even within nothingness itself, and so is not counted among the subtle ones. Furthermore: within the form realm, the heaven of no-thought is the very utmost; within the formless realm, neither perception nor non-perception is the very utmost. Within the Buddhadharma itself, there is properly the cessation of sensation and perception — the sphere of nothingness, among these three, is, in every case, not the superior concentration, and so is not taken as one of the three. Second, clarifying the factors; third, substance and function; fourth, depth; fifth, progress and regression; and sixth, merit — their sense may be understood by the same pattern as already given.

The inchworm and tied-bird similes are among this treatise's most memorable images precisely because they describe failure rather than success — a state genuinely more refined than anything before it, mistaken by non-Buddhist practitioners for the finish line itself, when it is in fact the very last rung of a ladder that still, eventually, runs out. The "true, imperishable spirit-self" critique directly names the ātman doctrine central to competing Indian traditions, diagnosed here as a subtle category error: mistaking the bare fact that something is aware of this refined state for evidence that an independent, permanent knower exists behind the awareness. The threefold taxonomy of "no-thought" — deviant, refined-but-still-ordinary, and the properly Buddhist cessation of sensation and perception — gives exact coordinates for a distinction the fascicle has been building toward since its opening aside on deviant no-thought concentration.

items.en: Why the Formless Concentrations Belong to Prajñā

zh: 般若滅一切法而能生一切法，如從初禪來滅憂，乃至非想非非想滅不用處之想，皆是般若中前方便，滅諸法為入空。以其滅諸法故，能生後勝法故，般若能生萬法故，此十二門禪皆般若氣分所攝。問曰：菩薩行菩提道，入實相空，尚不得空，今云何隨此不實顛倒之空分別有四耶？答曰：如《釋論》解四空義中說：「與諸法實相共智慧行，是四無色中，無有顛倒，是摩訶衍中四無色。」問曰：何等是諸法實相智？答曰：諸法自性空是。
en: Prajñā extinguishes every dharma and yet is able to give rise to every dharma as well — just as, proceeding from the first dhyāna onward, sorrow is extinguished, all the way through neither perception nor non-perception extinguishing even the very perception of the sphere of nothingness, all of this is precisely the preliminary expedient means within prajñā itself, extinguishing every dharma in order to enter emptiness. Because these dharmas are thus extinguished, later, superior dharma is able to be brought forth in turn — and, since prajñā itself is able to give rise to the ten thousand dharmas, these twelve gates of dhyāna are all encompassed within a partial share of prajñā, its preliminary portion.

Question: the bodhisattva, practicing the path to bodhi, enters the emptiness of the true mark itself, not even grasping at emptiness there — how, then, can it now be said that, following this unreal, inverted emptiness of the formless attainments, four distinct kinds are still distinguished? Answer: as the Exegetical Treatise explains in its own discussion of the meaning of the four emptinesses: "Practiced together with the wisdom of the true mark of all dharmas, these four formless attainments are free of any inversion at all — this is precisely the four formless attainments as understood within the Mahāyāna." Question: what, then, is this wisdom of the true mark of all dharmas? Answer: it is precisely that all dharmas are, of their own nature, empty.

zh:
問曰：色法和合，分別因緣故空，此無色中云何空？答曰：色是眼見耳聞，麁事能令空，何況不可見，無有對，不覺苦樂而不空耶？復次，色分別乃至微塵皆散滅歸空，是心心數法在日月時節乃至一念中不可得，是名真實四無色空義。菩薩如是知已，亦能分別種種諸相，以大悲方便為一切眾生故，行而不著。以此功德迴向菩提，具一切佛法，普施眾生，即是行菩薩道也。
釋禪波羅蜜次第法門卷第六
en: Question: form-dharmas, combining together, are distinguished as empty through their own causes and conditions — but how, then, can these formless attainments be said to be empty as well? Answer: form is what the eye sees and the ear hears — even this coarse matter can be shown to be empty; how much more, then, could what is invisible, without any resistance at all, and unfelt as either suffering or happiness, fail to be empty as well? Furthermore: form, analyzed down even to the finest particle, is entirely scattered and dissolved, returning to emptiness — and this very mind and its mental factors, examined across days, months, seasons, and even down to a single thought-moment, cannot be found at all either. This is what is truly meant by the emptiness of the four formless attainments.

The bodhisattva, having known this, is nonetheless still able to distinguish every kind of particular mark as well, and, through great compassion and skillful means, acts for the sake of all sentient beings without becoming attached to any of it. Dedicating this very merit toward bodhi, complete in the whole of the Buddhadharma, bestowing it universally upon sentient beings — this is precisely the practice of the bodhisattva path.
The Shi Chan Boluomi Cidi Famen, Fascicle Six, ends here.

This closing apologetic completes the argument fascicle 5 opened: dhyāna and prajñā are not two separate paths that need reconciling, because prajñā's own defining activity — extinguishing every dharma without becoming attached to the extinguishing — is exactly what every dhyāna already does at its own level, from the first dhyāna leaving behind sorrow to the formless attainments leaving behind perception itself. The "twelve gates of dhyāna" named here (the four dhyānas, four immeasurable minds, and four formless concentrations together) are thus reframed one final time as prajñā's own preliminary expedient means, not a lesser, contaminated detour from it. The extension of emptiness from form (visible, tangible, easy to doubt) to the formless attainments themselves (invisible, resistance-free, and thus even easier to mistake for something truly ultimate) closes the loop the earlier aside on deviant no-thought concentration and the inchworm simile both anticipated: the subtler an attainment feels, the more urgent it is not to mistake its subtlety for finality. This closes fascicle 6 in its entirety — the four immeasurable minds and the four formless concentrations complete, and, with them, the whole of mundane dhyāna (世間禪), the first of topic 7's four major divisions.

quiz.q: What does the second explanation of "neither perception nor non-perception" say?
options: the sphere of consciousness has perception and nothingness has none; "not perception" removes the former and "not non-perception" the latter
quiz.why: The second explanation removes both: "not perception" dispels the sphere of consciousness's perception, and "not non-perception" dispels nothingness's absence of it. B is the first explanation.

quiz.q: How does the Mahāyāna treatise reproach the sphere of nothingness?
options: consciousness is a wound and arrow, nothingness is delusion; both are illnesses of mind; there is a subtler concentration called "neither perception"
quiz.why: Nothingness is like delusion, intoxication, sleep, and darkness. The treatise calls both lower spheres illnesses of mind and seeks the subtler concentration.

quiz.q: Non-Buddhists take this concentration for nirvāṇa. What similes show they will fall back?
options: an inchworm reaching the branch tip turns back; a bird on a rope is pulled back when it runs out
quiz.why: Like an inchworm at the branch tip that must turn back, or a tethered bird pulled back when the rope runs out, since they do not know this concentration is the four aggregates combined.

quiz.q: What do non-Buddhists reckon the knowing mind in this concentration to be, and how does a disciple of the Buddha see it?
options: non-Buddhists take it as the true, imperishable spirit-self; disciples know it is the four aggregates, with no separate knowing spirit
quiz.why: Non-Buddhists take the knowing mind as the true, imperishable spirit-self; a disciple knows it is the four aggregates combined, deceptive and unreal, with no separate knowing spirit.

quiz.q: The text gives three senses of "no-thought." Who enters each?
options: non-Buddhists without skillful means: heaven of no-thought; ordinary practitioners with skillful means: neither perception nor non-perception; Buddha's disciples: cessation of sensation and perception
nothingness is one of the three
quiz.why: Non-Buddhists without skillful means enter the heaven of no-thought; those with some skillful means enter neither perception nor non-perception; disciples enter the cessation of sensation and perception. Nothingness is excluded.
